analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 100% tax on bonuses over $1 paid by companies that received TARP bailout money.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in March 2009 and never received a markup, a vote, or a single cosponsor before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After AIG and other bailed-out firms paid large bonuses using money from the 2008 federal rescue, this bill would have amended the tax code to tax executive bonuses at 100%, effectively returning the bonus money to the Treasury. It applied to any bonus over $1 paid by a company that received Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP) assistance, or that bought a business from one. The bill was sent to the tax-writing committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who funded the 2008 bailouts through the Treasury, would benefit if executive bonuses paid out of TARP-assisted firms were taxed back at 100%, with the revenue returning to the federal government. The bill was aimed at the executives whose bonuses became the symbol of the bailout's perceived unfairness.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the tax code to impose a 100% income tax on bonuses over $1 paid by entities that received financial assistance under TARP.

It defines the taxed amount as any aggregate payments 'in the nature of a bonus' from a TARP-assisted firm or from a business acquired from one, treating controlled groups including foreign corporations as a single employer, so bonus payments could not escape by shifting among affiliates.
The tax applies to taxable years ending after enactment, which would cover bonuses already paid during the year of the AIG bonus controversy.

By designating the revenue as a tax rather than a clawback contract term, the bill would have taken the money back without renegotiating individual employment contracts, which firms had argued legally obligated them to pay.
The bill's stated target, in its short title, is 'key executives' at AIG and other TARP-assisted firms — the people whose pay was underwritten by federal rescue funds.

analysis.who_pays: Executives and other employees of TARP-assisted companies would bear the full cost, owing tax equal to their entire bonus. The financial industry generally, and any firm that had received or acquired a business from a TARP recipient, would face the same tax on future bonus payments.

drawbacks.text: Because the effective date reaches the taxable year containing enactment, the bill would tax compensation — including the March 2009 AIG bonuses — after it had already been paid, raising the fairness and legal objections that apply to retroactive taxation, objections that were raised against the similar 90% bonus-tax bill the House considered that month.

Despite its title focusing on 'key executives,' the text taxes any bonus over $1 from any current or former TARP recipient or any business acquired from one, which reaches well beyond AIG's top brass and could sweep in ordinary employees of rescued firms, including acquired units.

A 100% marginal tax on bonuses gives TARP-assisted firms a strong incentive to restructure compensation into base salary or other untaxed forms, potentially defeating the bill's purpose while leaving the distortion in place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — taxing back bonuses paid by firms living on federal rescue money — was one of the most popular responses to the 2009 bonus controversy, and the mechanism is simple and directly recovers taxpayer money. But the bill as written is blunt: it is effectively retroactive to bonuses already paid, it reaches far beyond the executives it names, and a 100% rate invites compensation restructuring. A narrower, prospective clawback would have captured most of the benefit with fewer of those defects. As introduced, the bill died with no cosponsors and no committee action, so none of these design questions were ever tested or refined.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Gwen Moore introduced the bill on March 18, 2009, amid the controversy over bonuses paid by AIG and other firms that had received federal bailout assistance.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, and no further action — no hearings, no markup, no floor vote — ever appears in its history.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors during its two years in Congress.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill died in committee, as all bills introduced but not passed do at the end of a Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives and employees of AIG and other TARP-assisted firms were better off: no bonus tax was ever enacted, and the bonuses at issue stayed in recipients' hands untaxed. Ways and Means members who might have faced a floor vote on a popular bonus tax were also spared one.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: AIG and TARP-firm executives kept their bonuses

for.name: Rep. Gwen Moore
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 18, 2009 and gave introductory remarks, proposing a 100% tax on TARP-firm bonuses.

for.name: Ways and Means Committee Democrats
for.role: Committee of jurisdiction (253 House Democrats in the majority)
for.what_they_did: Held the bill's referral; no member of the majority committee took it up, and no markup was ever scheduled.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on March 18, 2009 and never reported it out; no hearing, markup, or vote on the bill appears in its history.

against.name: Charles Rangel
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of jurisdiction, never brought the bill to a markup or a committee vote.

against.name: AIG and other TARP-assisted financial firms
against.role: Recipients of federal bailout funds whose bonuses were targeted
against.what_they_did: Opposed bonus-recapture measures in this period; the bill died without ever reaching a vote in which they would have had to defend the payments publicly.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held and the bill had zero cosponsors, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and a Democratic-controlled committee's inaction; no party breakdown of support or opposition exists.

industries.industry: Executives and employees at TARP-assisted financial firms
industries.note: The bill would have taxed 100% of their bonuses over $1, taking back pay funded partly by federal rescue money. The bill's death left the bonuses in place.

industries.industry: Banks and companies that received TARP funds or bought businesses from them
industries.note: These firms would have faced the tax on all future bonus payments and a strong incentive to restructure pay. The bill's reach extended to acquirers of TARP-firm business units, not just the original recipients.

With this bill and the similar bonus-tax proposals of March 2009 dying without becoming law, executive bonus practices at bailout-assisted firms faced no tax recapture, leaving the pay structure that angered the public intact.
